top.headline: Miami Judge Rules Federal Noncitizen Voting Law Unconstitutional
top.blurb: A federal judge in Miami dismissed a case against a Jamaican-born Florida resident charged with voting in the 2020 election, ruling that only states, not Congress, can set voter qualifications under the Constitution. It is the first time a federal court has struck down the 1996 law, though the ruling binds only this case and roughly 45 similar prosecutions remain pending nationwide.

top.headline: Tennessee Halts Executions After Death Row Inmate Survives Lethal Injection
top.blurb: Tennessee officials administered two doses of lethal drugs to Christa Gail Pike, who would have been the state's first woman executed in over 200 years, but she remained alive and was taken to a hospital by ambulance. Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review and paused the state's remaining executions for the rest of the year, calling the failure unprecedented.

top.headline: Delhi Police Block Protest Demanding Chief Election Commissioner's Resignation
top.blurb: Police barricaded Jantar Mantar, shut a dozen metro stations and detained roughly 500 protesters — including AAP leaders and student groups — demonstrating for CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and a rollback of the voter-roll revision. The protest followed reports that two of the Election Commission's own commissioners had repeatedly objected to decisions made without their knowledge.

top.headline: Karnataka Finds Hospitals Marking Up Cancer Drugs by Up to 52 Times Their Cost
top.blurb: A Karnataka government inspection found 253 medicines with 'extreme pricing anomalies,' including a cancer drug bought by hospitals for ₹86 and billed to patients at ₹4,528 — a 52-fold markup. The state has sought central intervention after finding patients routinely billed near the printed MRP while hospitals received steep institutional discounts from manufacturers.

top.headline: US Sends Third Aircraft Carrier Toward Iran as War Enters Eighth Month
top.blurb: A US official told Al Jazeera that a third aircraft carrier is being deployed toward waters near Iran, deepening the American military presence as the US-Israel war against Iran drags into its eighth month. The move comes as Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded Iran's delegation leave the UN General Assembly after ceasefire talks stalled.

top.headline: Senior UN Food Agency Official Says He Lost His Job Over Gaza Criticism
top.blurb: Ben Davis, a 26-year veteran of the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, says his contract was not renewed after he helped organize staff silences over Gaza's famine and worked on a report referencing humanitarian law that superiors ordered taken down. The agency's director-general has separately warned staff against 'playing the political game' on human rights.

top.headline: Shubman Gill Smashes Fastest-Ever ODI Double Century in Record Chase
top.blurb: India's captain blazed to an unbeaten 223 off 133 balls, reaching 200 in just 117 deliveries to break the record for cricket's fastest ODI double century, as India ran down West Indies' 405 with 39 balls to spare in Guwahati. Gill is now the only man to have scored double hundreds in both Tests and ODIs as captain.

top.headline: 'My Sad Dead' Is Unlike Anything Else on Television
top.blurb: Mercedes Morán stars as an antisocial doctor who can see and speak with ghosts in this four-part Spanish-language miniseries, directed by Pablo Larraín and drawn from three stories by 'the sorceress of Buenos Aires horror,' Mariana Enriquez. NPR calls its mix of creepiness, melancholy, dark comedy and political anger unlike anything else on TV right now.

bengal.headline: Kolkata Police Submit Report on Film School Clash Between Students and RSS-Linked Group
bengal.blurb: Kolkata Police submitted a six-page report on last week's violence at the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute, saying roughly 250 people were identified and 23 interrogated from both the student and ABGP sides.

bengal.headline: Congress Leader Urges Mamata Banerjee to Return and Lead Bengal Unit
bengal.blurb: Senior Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury suggested Mamata Banerjee return to the Congress fold and lead its Bengal unit, as the Trinamool Congress grapples with a leadership crisis after its defeat in this year's assembly election.

travel.headline: 10 Best Places to Visit in October
travel.blurb: Lonely Planet's October picks range from balmy seas in Menorca, the Seychelles and Fiji to Montenegro's peaks, Tōhoku's turning forests, Morocco's Fez and Peru's Cuzco for history seekers.

travel.headline: Five Orphaned Orangutans Found in an Odisha Forest Face a Long Road Home
travel.blurb: Five infant orangutans found wandering an Odisha forest in September may have been trafficked across borders from Sumatra, and now face a slow bureaucratic journey through Indian and Indonesian wildlife law before any return home.

happy.headline: Ancient Roman Treasures Lay Hidden Beneath the Ballroom Where Jane Austen Danced
happy.blurb: While Jane Austen twirled through Bath's Assembly Rooms two centuries ago, Roman coins, pottery, glassware and a military helmet fragment lay undisturbed in the ground beneath her feet — only unearthed now that renovations have let archaeologists dig below the historic ballroom.

tech_top.headline: Trump and Tech CEOs Rebrand AI as 'Super Intelligence,' Sign Voluntary Safety Accord
tech_top.blurb: President Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to refer to AI as 'Super Intelligence,' while the chiefs of Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Tesla and SpaceX signed a voluntary White House accord promising layered internal monitoring and independent audits. The pledge carries no legal force — Trump called it 'morally binding' — and critics say it leaves AI safety more unsettled than before.
tech_top.pm_note: A rebrand plus a voluntary pledge is a governance signal, not a regulation — track the follow-through (internal monitoring, independent audits) rather than the name change itself.

tech_top.headline: OpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers Over Leaked Information, WSJ Reports
tech_top.blurb: OpenAI dismissed two safety researchers and a program manager after an internal probe found they shared confidential company information with an outside AI-safety organization that tests models. The move follows a New York Times report that OpenAI executives dismissed employee warnings about security practices, amid a string of incidents involving the company's AI agents.
tech_top.pm_note: When an internal safety team's own members start leaking to outside watchdogs, treat it as a signal your escalation channels aren't trusted internally — not just a personnel problem.

tech_top.headline: Mandiant Founder's 'Agent Swarm' Security Startup Raises $255.5M at $2.5B Valuation
tech_top.blurb: Kevin Mandia's Armadin, which runs always-on autonomous AI agents that chain together vulnerabilities to break into client systems before attackers do, raised a $255.5 million round led by Andreessen Horowitz and Accel. The round values the six-month-old approach to continuous, agentic penetration testing at over $2.5 billion, more than double its March valuation.
tech_top.pm_note: Continuous agentic red-teaming is becoming a category of its own — worth evaluating against point-in-time pen tests if your security budget still assumes annual audits are enough.

tech_more.headline: Trump and Big AI Are Betting Trillions on the Same Industrial Revolution
tech_more.blurb: Axios maps the shared bet between the White House and AI labs that trillions in chip, data-center and power spending will pay off in productivity gains — even as hyperscalers have already spent nearly $1 trillion more on AI infrastructure since 2024 than the technology has generated in revenue.

tech_more.headline: Amazon's Redesigned Kindle Ditches Its Bezel for a Flush-Front Display
tech_more.blurb: Amazon's biggest Kindle redesign in years drops the raised bezel for a flush front, using capacitive touch and haptics to avoid accidental taps, with the base model now 6.8mm thick, 140 grams and 30% faster at turning pages.

tech_101.text: In September 2026 the Trump administration began requiring federal agencies to call AI 'Super Intelligence' instead, while the underlying legal definition of artificial intelligence stays the same. Renaming a technology doesn't change what it does — watch whether the substance (safety testing, audits, liability) changes along with the label, or only the label does.

Traditional penetration testing uses a small team to probe a system once or twice a year. 'Agent swarm' security tools instead run many autonomous AI agents continuously, each hunting for and chaining together vulnerabilities the way a real attacker would — trading a periodic snapshot for always-on coverage, at the cost of trusting an AI agent with deep system access.

science.headline: A Modified Sugar Molecule Could Enable a New Class of Water-Soluble Plastics
science.blurb: Chemists converted trehalose — a sugar that lets some organisms survive extreme drying — into a polymerizable building block, then used it to make water-soluble polymers with precisely controllable amounts of sugar built into their structure. The platform gives materials scientists a new, tunable way to design sugar-based polymers for future biomedical and industrial uses.

science.headline: NASA's Crew-13 Sets Speed Record Docking at the Space Station
science.blurb: A SpaceX Dragon carrying NASA, Canadian and Russian crew members docked at the International Space Station just 7 hours and 55 minutes after launch — the fastest trip to orbit ever flown by an American spacecraft, beating the old record by about five hours. The four joined the Expedition 75 crew for a six-month stay.

science.headline: A Diet Rich in Berries and Greens May Slow Brain Aging by Years
science.blurb: A 12-year Framingham Heart Study analysis found that adults who more closely followed the MIND diet — a Mediterranean-DASH hybrid emphasizing berries, leafy greens and poultry — showed about 20% less grey-matter shrinkage per three-point increase in diet score, equivalent to roughly 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Sweets and fried fast food were linked to greater tissue loss over the same period.

philosophy.headline: Why Real Intelligence Is Something More Than Optimization
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Sasha Mudd argues that defining intelligence purely as optimization toward a goal hands enormous power to whoever sets that goal — a concern sharpened by AI systems built explicitly to optimize. Real intelligence, she argues, requires the capacity to question whether the objective itself deserves pursuing, not just skill at achieving it.

philosophy.headline: Good Science Requires More Than Just Evidence
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher David Kyle Johnson argues that evidence alone has never been enough to judge a scientific theory — qualities like parsimony and explanatory scope have always done real work in deciding between theories that fit the same data. The piece is a reminder that 'follow the evidence' understates how much judgment science actually requires.

philosophy_101.text: Beyond fitting the evidence, philosophers of science judge theories by qualities like parsimony (fewer assumptions), scope (explaining more), and fruitfulness (predicting new findings) — the 'theoretical virtues' that help choose between rival theories that explain the same data equally well.

To optimize is to maximize or minimize some single measurable quantity — a chess engine optimizes for winning positions, an ad algorithm for clicks. Defining intelligence as optimization is useful for building AI, but critics note it says nothing about whether the goal being optimized for is itself a good one.
